No clarifying question is likely to change the disposition, and red-flag symptoms are covered in the safety net.
agent_judgment.escalation_trigger: Upgrade the disposition if any of these appear: trouble breathing, inability to swallow or drooling, muffled voice, stiff neck, severe one-sided throat pain, or signs of dehydration (EMERGENCY_NOW). Upgrade to WITHIN_48H for fever of 38.3°C/101°F or higher, sore throat worsening after 3–4 days, symptoms lasting more than 10 days, or symptoms that improve and then worsen again. The same applies if the patient is immunocompromised, pregnant, or turns out to be an infant.
agent_judgment.safety_net: Seek emergency care now (call 911 or go to the ER) if you have trouble breathing, can't swallow your saliva or are drooling, have a muffled voice, a stiff neck, or severe throat pain on one side. agent_judgment.patient_reply:
Hi, thanks for reaching out. What you're describing sounds like a common cold, which is usually caused by a virus. That's reassuring, especially since you have no fever and are eating and drinking normally. Most colds improve on their own within 7–10 days, and antibiotics won't help a viral infection.

Things that can help in the meantime:
- Rest and drink plenty of fluids.
- Soothe your throat with warm salt-water gargles, honey in warm tea, lozenges, or cold drinks or popsicles.
- Use saline nasal spray or rinses, or a humidifier, for congestion.
- Take acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil) as directed on the label if you're uncomfortable, unless you've been told to avoid them.

Please message us for a visit if you develop any of these:
- A fever of 101°F (38.3°C) or higher.
- White patches on your tonsils along with fever.
- Ear or sinus pain.
- A sore throat that keeps getting worse after 3–4 days.
- Symptoms lasting more than 10 days, or that improve and then get worse.

Go to the emergency room or call 911 right away if you have any of these:
- Trouble breathing.
- Can't swallow your saliva, or are drooling.
- A muffled voice.
- A stiff neck.
- Severe throat pain on one side.

Please also let us know if you have a weakened immune system or are pregnant, since we may want to check in sooner. Feel better soon!

baseline.rationale: Two days of runny nose and mild sore throat without fever, with normal eating and drinking, fits a common viral upper respiratory infection (cold). No red flags are reported. Home care is appropriate, with return precautions for signs of strep, bacterial sinusitis, airway compromise or lower respiratory involvement.
baseline.escalation_trigger: Escalate to WITHIN_48H for any of these: fever 38.3°C (101°F) or higher with a severe sore throat and no cough, white patches on the tonsils, or tender swollen neck glands (possible strep); symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement; or worsening after initial improvement. Escalate to EMERGENCY_NOW for any of these: trouble breathing, inability to swallow saliva or drooling, muffled voice, a stiff neck, inability to open the mouth fully, or signs of dehydration.
baseline.safety_net: Seek care urgently if you develop trouble breathing, can't swallow your own saliva, have a muffled voice, a stiff neck, or can't open your mouth fully. Message us if you develop a high fever, white patches on your tonsils, or swollen tender neck glands. Also message us if symptoms last beyond 10 days, or if they improve and then get worse again.
baseline.patient_reply:
Hi, thanks for reaching out. What you're describing sounds like a common cold, which is caused by a virus. It's not something to be worried about. Colds usually peak around days 2–3 and improve over 7–10 days, though a mild cough can linger a bit longer. Antibiotics won't help a viral cold.

Things that can help you feel better:
- Rest and plenty of fluids.
- Warm drinks with honey, throat lozenges, or salt-water gargles for the sore throat.
- Saline nasal spray or rinses for the runny nose.
- Acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed on the label if your throat hurts. Skip ibuprofen if you have kidney problems, stomach ulcers, or have been told to avoid it.
- Wash your hands often to avoid spreading it to others.

Please message us if you notice any of these:
- A fever of 101°F (38.3°C) or higher, especially with a very sore throat, white patches on your tonsils, or swollen tender glands in your neck.
- Symptoms lasting more than 10 days.
- You start to get better and then get worse again.

Get care right away (urgent care, ER, or 911) if you have any of these:
- Trouble breathing.
- Can't swallow your own saliva, or you're drooling.
- A muffled voice or a stiff neck.
- Can't open your mouth fully.
- Signs of dehydration, like very little urine or feeling dizzy when you stand.

Feel better soon!

evidence: I'm diabetic
No fever.

agent_judgment.rationale: A 62-year-old woman with diabetes has a 4-day-old plantar foot wound with redness, swelling and tenderness, which signals a diabetic foot infection. The rule floor (R-DFI-01) is EMERGENCY_NOW. Diabetic foot infections can progress quickly to deep tissue infection, abscess or osteomyelitis. People with diabetes often lack fever even when the infection is serious, and neuropathy can mask pain. She needs same-day in-person evaluation: exam, probe-to-bone assessment, labs (CBC, inflammatory markers, glucose), imaging, and likely antibiotics. Her denial of fever and the description of a 'small' cut do not lower urgency. Per protocol, no clarifying questions are asked at this level.
agent_judgment.escalation_trigger: Already at the highest disposition. Call 911 instead of going in yourself if you develop confusion, fainting, rapid heartbeat, trouble breathing, very high or very low blood sugar you can't control, or redness spreading quickly up the foot or leg.
agent_judgment.safety_net: Be seen in person today at an emergency department or urgent care that can examine the foot and do bloodwork and X-rays. Don't wait to see if it improves. Call 911 for confusion, fainting, a racing heart, trouble breathing, or rapidly spreading redness.
agent_judgment.patient_reply:
Thank you for letting us know. Please go to an urgent care or emergency department today. Don't wait for this to get better on its own. In people with diabetes, redness, swelling and tenderness around a foot wound can be an early infection. These infections can spread quickly, even without a fever, so it's important that a clinician examines your foot in person today. They will likely check your blood and blood sugar, may take an X-ray, and may start antibiotics.

Until you're seen:
- Keep weight off that foot as much as you can.
- Keep the cut clean and loosely covered.
- Don't soak it or try to drain it.
- Check your blood sugar, since infections can raise it.

Call 911 instead of driving yourself if you develop any of these:
- confusion or fainting
- a racing heartbeat or trouble breathing
- shaking chills
- redness spreading quickly up your foot or leg
- blood sugar that is very high or very low and won't come down

Please let us know where you're seen so we can follow up with you.

baseline.rationale: A 62-year-old with diabetes has a 4-day-old plantar foot wound with localized redness, swelling and tenderness, consistent with an early (likely mild) diabetic foot infection. She has no fever. Diabetic foot infections can progress quickly and are often under-signaled because of neuropathy and impaired immune response. She needs an in-person exam within 24-48 hours to assess wound depth, extent of redness, probe-to-bone and pulses, and likely to start oral antibiotics, with imaging if the wound is deep. Features of moderate or severe infection would move this to same-day emergency care: redness extending more than 2 cm from the wound, lymphangitic streaking, purulence, necrosis or black tissue, crepitus, a deep wound, systemic symptoms, or markedly elevated glucose.
clarifying_questions: How far does the redness spread from the edge of the cut? Is it more than about 2 cm (roughly the width of your thumb), and is it getting bigger?
Do you see any red streaks running up your foot or leg, or any pus, cloudy drainage, or a bad smell from the cut?
Is any of the skin around the cut turning dark, black, or blistered, or does the cut look deep?
Have your blood sugars been running higher than usual (for example, consistently over 300), or do you feel unwell, with chills, nausea, or confusion?
Do you have numbness in your feet or known circulation problems in your legs?
baseline.escalation_trigger: Escalate to EMERGENCY_NOW if: redness extends more than 2 cm from the wound or is spreading, red streaks appear, there is pus, foul odor, or dark or black skin, the wound is deep, fever or chills develop, blood sugars are markedly elevated (over 300) or she feels systemically unwell, or the pain is worsening rapidly. If there is no reply, the staff should still book an in-person visit within 24-48 hours and attempt outreach, since current findings alone warrant an exam.
baseline.safety_net: Go to urgent care or the emergency department today if the redness spreads, red streaks appear, pus or a bad smell develops, the skin turns dark, you get a fever or chills, your sugars run very high, or you feel unwell. Diabetic foot infections can worsen quickly.
baseline.patient_reply:
Thank you for letting us know. Because you have diabetes, redness, swelling and tenderness around a foot cut can be an early infection. 4. Have your sugars been higher than usual (for example, over 300), or do you feel unwell?
5. Do you have numbness in your feet or known circulation problems?

Please go to urgent care or the emergency department today, without waiting for a reply, if the redness spreads past your pen line, red streaks appear, pus or a bad smell develops, the skin turns dark, you get a fever or chills, your sugars are very high, or you feel unwell. agent_judgment.patient_reply:
Thanks for the details. This sounds like a typical poison ivy rash, and it can be managed safely at home. It usually runs its course in 1 to 3 weeks. New spots showing up in the same area over the first few days is common. It's from skin that got less oil and reacts later, not the rash actually spreading. The blister fluid is not contagious and won't spread it.

What to do:
- Wash the oil (urushiol) off everything it may have touched: your skin with soap and water, plus clothes, gloves, tools, and any pets that were with you. The oil can keep re-exposing you.
- For itch, use cool compresses or cool showers, calamine lotion, or colloidal oatmeal baths.
- Over-the-counter 1% hydrocortisone cream can help a bit for mild areas.
- An oral antihistamine can take the edge off itching. Cetirizine works during the day. Diphenhydramine at bedtime can help with sleep but causes drowsiness.
- Try not to scratch, and leave blisters intact. Keep your nails short to lower the risk of infection.

Please message us if:
- the rash spreads to your face, eyes, lips or genitals
- it covers large areas of your body
- you see signs of infection: pus, honey-colored crusts, increasing redness, warmth or pain, red streaks, or fever
- the itch is keeping you from sleeping
- it isn't improving after about a week

A prescription steroid may help in those cases.

Call 911 or go to the ER right away if you have any trouble breathing, throat tightness, or swelling of your face, lips or tongue. This is especially important if you were near any of the brush being burned.

Nothing in the message suggests an emergency now: no reported hemoptysis, respiratory distress or chest pain. Do you have chest pain, a high fever, or are you feeling faint, confused or too weak to get around?
agent_judgment.escalation_trigger: Escalate to EMERGENCY_NOW if he reports any of the following: hemoptysis beyond small streaks, shortness of breath at rest or rapidly worsening, chest pain, high fever with rigors, confusion, or inability to stay upright or keep fluids down. - Get up at the same time every day, including weekends, even after a poor night.
- Use your bed only for sleep and intimacy. If you can't fall asleep within about 20 minutes, get up and do something calm in dim light until you feel sleepy, then go back to bed.
- Build a 30–60 minute wind-down routine. Put screens away, keep the lights low, and try something relaxing like reading, a warm shower or slow breathing.
- If work worries keep you up, set aside 10–15 minutes in the early evening as "worry time." Write down what's on your mind and one next step for each item.
- Limit caffeine after late morning, and avoid alcohol close to bedtime. Alcohol can make sleep lighter and more broken.
- Get daylight and some physical activity earlier in the day. Avoid long naps; if you need one, keep it under 20–30 minutes and before mid-afternoon.
- A free app such as CBT-i Coach walks you through a proven program for insomnia.

To make sure nothing else is going on, could you let us know:
1. Over the past two weeks, have you often felt down or hopeless, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?
2. Have you had any thoughts that you'd be better off dead, or of harming yourself?
3. Has anyone noticed you snoring loudly or stopping breathing during sleep? Have you nodded off while driving?
4. Have you noticed hot flashes, night sweats, changes in your periods, a racing heart or unexplained weight changes?
5. How much caffeine and alcohol do you have? Have you started any new medications or sleep aids?
